_about: The mystery deck's content. Written by Lyra on the date of this file's commit, from the unreserved list in the private facilitator pack and the verified table in docs/site-spec.md. Builders render this file and NEVER change its words. Every non-fictional card cites a verified source on its reveal side. Exactly one card is fictional (fictional: true): render it with data-fictional="true" and show its fiction_notice on the reveal.
intro: Each card is a claim. Look at it, predict whether it holds up, then turn it over. You don't score by being right; the deck rewards predicting before you look.

cards.title: Emergence?
cards.mystery: A language model solved 93% of classic theory-of-mind tasks. Has theory of mind spontaneously emerged?
cards.inspect: Classic tasks are famous, and famous puzzles can be recognised rather than reasoned through. What would happen with control versions added: the same kind of story, changed so the famous answer is wrong?
cards.reveal: The same model, tested properly, solved about 20%. The batteries differ, so this is not the same test scored twice. It is what proper controls do to a headline.

cards.title: Selected for the trend
cards.mystery: Here are 11 tasks where bigger language models do worse. Is bigger really worse on them?
cards.inspect: These tasks were collected because they showed the trend. What happens one step further up in scale?
cards.reveal: At 540 billion parameters, only 4 of the 11 still got worse, and 6 turned U-shaped: worse, then better. A trend picked out for its shape can stop at the edge of the sample.

cards.title: Being wrong well
cards.mystery: Forecasters predicted 12.7% on a hard maths benchmark (MATH) for mid-2022. Did they get close?
cards.inspect: Compare the forecast with the score that was actually measured in mid-2022.
cards.reveal: The measured score was 50.3%. The researcher who commissioned the forecasts published his own surprise, in public. Saying plainly that you were wrong is part of the method.

cards.title: A goal, missed, said plainly
cards.mystery: A lab set out to build a classifier that never lets an injurious completion through. Did they reach it?
cards.inspect: Read the lab's own write-up of the result.
cards.reveal: In their own words: "we fell well short of that target". A lab reporting its miss as clearly as a win is rarer than it should be, and worth copying.

cards.title: A true one
cards.mystery: Language models use information in the middle of a long context worse than information at its start or end. True?
cards.inspect: Look at the curve: accuracy against where the relevant document sits in the context.
cards.reveal: True. Accuracy is highest when the answer is near the beginning or the end, and dips in the middle. Not every surprising claim is a trap; calibration means believing the ones that hold.

sources.label: Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle", arXiv:2307.03172

cards.title: The greenhouse chart
cards.mystery: In a greenhouse trial, 3,000 houseplants played two hours of podcasts a day grew taller than plants kept in silence. The chart shows them reaching 35 metres. Something on this chart is wrong. Can you fix it?
cards.inspect: Look at the units on the height axis. Houseplants are not 35 metres tall.
cards.reveal: Nicely caught: the axis should say centimetres, not metres. But there's a bigger problem.
cards.fiction_notice: This study is invented. There was never a houseplant podcast trial. You fixed a unit inside a claim nobody ever made. Before you polish a citation, check that its source exists.

closing.question: Did you spot the false premise?
closing.body: One card corrected a detail inside a claim that was itself made up. Fixing what's in front of you is easy to reward; questioning the frame is the harder habit. Neither answer is a score: noticing is the point.
